| [THEORY-128](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-128.md) | After mass bleaching, coral recovery on a reef crest depends on large herbivorous fishes keeping macroalgae down, because recovery runs through recruitment and survival that macroalgae suppress, not through the persistence of surviving colonies alone | Hughes et al. (2007), [LIT-711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-711.md). On the reef crest at Orpheus Island after the 1998 bleaching, four roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae averaged 56% cover inside against 4.1% and 1.7% in controls. Coral cover reached 7.7% inside against 19.2% and 20.2%, with recruitment about two-thirds lower and mortality of established colonies more than double. Control recovery came mainly from recruits of taxa bleaching had removed. Proposed: one site, four replicates, plot scale, and fish exclusion standing in for herbivore exclusion. The algal state vanished within 30 days of reopening. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-130](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-130.md) | Coral bleaching is the breakdown of a regulated host–symbiont exchange, reached by more than one route, not a single mechanism of symbiont loss | Two reviews, with no data of their own. Boilard et al. (2020), [LIT-712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-712.md), collect the regulators of the coral–dinoflagellate exchange: the host controls symbiont density, bacteria shift the nitrogen supply, and heat leads either to host rejection of symbionts (apoptosis, autophagy, exocytosis, detachment, necrosis) or to pigment loss under oxidative stress. Goulet et al. (2020), [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md), report two octocorals whose similar symbiont losses at +3 °C came by different routes, one by fewer symbionts per host cell and one by loss of host cells. Proposed. The claim that the wider microbiome drives bleaching is declined: its own source says it cannot yet be tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-132.md) | Stability, a system's speed of return to equilibrium after disturbance, and resilience, its capacity to absorb change and persist within its domain of attraction, are distinct properties that can trade off, so a system can be highly unstable and highly resilient, and managing it for constancy can erode its resilience | Holling (1973), [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md). Stability is return to equilibrium. Resilience is persistence under change, set by the extent of the domain of attraction and the system's distance from its edge. Budworm forests and insect populations in harsh climates are unstable and resilient; homogeneous lakes are stable and fragile. Active for the distinction, which has become standard. The claim that management for constancy erodes resilience rests on suggestive cases. | Active |
| [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md) v2 | A persistent or abrupt change is not evidence that a system has alternative stable states: field patterns such as jumps, multimodality and dual relationships also arise from a stepwise driver or a simple threshold, and only hysteresis, initial-state dependence or a lasting shift after a temporary disturbance, with slow return excluded, comes close to showing one | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md). Alternative attractors predict sudden shifts, multimodal states and dual responses to a driver, and so do discontinuous drivers and threshold responses. Discriminating evidence is experimental: different starting states reaching different end states, temporary disturbances causing lasting shifts, or hysteresis. Slow recovery can mimic all three. Positive feedback must be strong to produce alternative states. Active as a methodological standard. | Active |
| [THEORY-469](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-469.md) | Because persistence (mean absolute fitness at least 1) and selection (fitness differences) are logically independent, niche construction theory's evolutionary niche, read externally as the factors producing fitness differences in a population, differs in extension from the realized population ecological niche even after unit and modality are matched, so it is not a simple translation of Hutchinson's niche | Trappes (2021), [LIT-169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-169.md), read in [NOTE-155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-155.md). The non-identity follows from a conceptual argument the reading grades strong. The three kinds of case that populate the gap are weaker: habitat degradation rests on a projected persistence failure, commensalism on one field study after the author's first candidate failed, and non-limiting resources on a "possible example". The result is scoped to Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman's 2003 niche concept and to the externalist reading of selection pressure. It does not say the two niches differ much; they "still coincide to a large extent". | Active |
| [THEORY-473](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-473.md) | Scaled down to one organism, Hutchinson's niche, defined as the conditions that give that individual an expected lifetime reproductive success of at least one, is observed only as a point; the rest of it is counterfactual, reached by translocation in only a few dimensions and otherwise inferred from other individuals, so in practice it is the niche of a phenotype class, and its authors call it mostly metaphorical | Takola & Schielzeth (2022), [LIT-127](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-127.md), read in full in [NOTE-170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-170.md). The working definition (p. 5) gives the individualized niche an absolute-fitness boundary, expected LRS ≥ 1, and splits it into realized, potential, time-slice, prospective and trajectory-based niches. That the realized niche is a point and the potential niche unobservable follows from the definitions. The paper concedes there is "no empirical solution" at the individual level (p. 15), and its fix, marginalizing fitness functions across individuals, is schematic. It is a framework for structuring research, by its authors' own account, not a measurement. | Active |
| [THEORY-548](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-548.md) | A delay in the interactions of a large random Lotka–Volterra community whose undelayed equilibrium is feasible and globally stable destabilises it through a Hopf bifurcation at a critical delay set by the community spectrum, giving sustained oscillation with no external forcing; whether diversity then stabilises depends on the measure, since in the oscillating regime community-level variability falls with diversity while species-level variability rises | Saeedian et al. (2021), [LIT-057](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-057.md), a preprint, read in [NOTE-061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-061.md). The critical delay is the standard linear delay result applied to a random community matrix, and matched simulation at one parameter setting (strong self-regulation, d_B = 10, σ_B = 0.1, C = 1). It falls with diversity S, which [NOTE-061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-061.md) suggests may be an extreme-value effect of the growth rates rather than of interactions. The diversity result rests on two delays and S ≲ 70, with no test against the averaging null the paper itself cites. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-560](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-560.md) | In rodents, gut microbes can drive stress and affect-related behaviour through vagal, immune, endocrine and metabolite routes, and faecal transplant from depressed people partly transfers the phenotype; in people, probiotics have so far shown at most small reductions in subjective stress in healthy volunteers, and strains with strong preclinical records have failed in controlled trials | Forssten et al. (2022), [LIT-915](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-915.md), read in [NOTE-703](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-703.md). A narrative review with no search method, by employees of a probiotics manufacturer, which documents its own translational failures: L. rhamnosus JB-1 had no effect on any outcome against placebo after "comprehensive preclinical evidence". The rodent half is well documented; the human half rests on one meta-analysis of healthy volunteers and trials with nulls. Proposed because the source is a narrative industry review; the gap it describes runs against its authors' interest. | Proposed |
